---
title: "Autocorrelation in a Markov chain"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The chains for the passage-level Student-t model agree across initializations, but adjacent draws remain dependent. **Autocorrelation** measures the association between a saved sequence and a shifted copy of itself.

For a stationary scalar sequence, the autocorrelation at lag $t$ is

$$
\rho_t
=
\operatorname{Corr}(\Theta_s,\Theta_{s+t}).
$$

Lag one compares adjacent draws; lag ten compares draws ten transitions apart. A chain of 1,000 draws supplies 999 lag-one pairs and 990 lag-ten pairs.

## The production passage-level Student-t model autocorrelation functions

```{r}
#| label: compute-provo-autocorrelation
library(ggplot2)
library(posterior)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cache <- readRDS(
  "data/provo/provo-stan-draw-cache.rds"
)
draws <- as.data.frame(as_draws_df(subset_draws(
  cache$production_draws, variable = c("mu", "sigma")
)))

acf_rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("mu", "sigma"), function(parameter) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(split(draws, draws$.chain), function(chain_data) {
    values <- as.numeric(acf(chain_data[[parameter]], lag.max = 40L,
                             plot = FALSE, demean = TRUE)$acf)
    data.frame(parameter, chain = chain_data$.chain[1], lag = 0:40,
               autocorrelation = values)
  }))
}))

stopifnot(nrow(provo) == 55L, nrow(draws) == 4000L,
          all(abs(acf_rows$autocorrelation[acf_rows$lag == 0] - 1) < 1e-12))
subset(acf_rows, lag <= 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-autocorrelation
#| fig-cap: "Within-chain autocorrelation for the production draws from the passage-level Student-t posterior."
ggplot(acf_rows,
       aes(lag, autocorrelation, group = factor(chain), color = factor(chain))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey75", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .55) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, ncol = 1) +
  scale_color_grey(start = .15, end = .7) +
  labs(x = "Lag", y = "Autocorrelation", color = "Chain") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Rapid decay suggests that dependence weakens over a small number of transitions. Slow decay means that information about one state persists across later states. High autocorrelation need not imply the wrong stationary distribution, but it reduces finite-run precision.

Negative autocorrelation can make alternating values offset one another and improve precision for some averages. Thus the complete sequence matters, not only lag one. Thinning may make the retained sequence look less correlated, but it discards information and creates none.

Autocorrelation diagnoses the numerical sequence. It does not describe dependence among readers, word positions, or passages in the underlying Provo study.

## Check your understanding

1. How many lag-25 pairs occur in one 1,000-draw chain?
2. What does slow ACF decay imply about finite-run information?
3. Why can a correct chain have positive autocorrelation?
4. Why does thinning not create information?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. There are $1000-25=975$ lag-25 pairs. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Slow decay means that many saved states carry overlapping information, reducing finite-run precision and ESS. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Stationarity determines the marginal target, not independence; a valid transition can preserve the target while moving locally between correlated states. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Thinning discards saved states. It may lower correlation among retained neighbors, but it cannot add information absent from the original chain. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [effective-sample-size page](effective-sample-size.qmd) translates this dependence into an information-equivalent draw count.
